meta.title: The Last Ferry to Millbrook
meta.genre: Cozy small-town mystery with a touch of the uncanny
meta.tone: Warm and welcoming on the surface, with a quiet, accumulating wrongness underneath
meta.synopsis: The last ferry of the season drops you in Millbrook just as the fog rolls in — and doesn't leave. The town is friendly, the inn is warm, and everyone insists nothing is wrong. But the ferry isn't due back for a week, and you're starting to notice that no one in Millbrook quite agrees on what happened yesterday.
content_rules: PG-13 (mild peril and tension, no graphic violence)
keep the uncanny atmospheric and suggestive rather than graphic or gory

style: Let the ordinary linger just long enough to feel safe before a small detail undercuts it - warmth and unease sit in the same paragraph.
Dialogue should feel unhurried and genuinely warm on the surface; the wrongness lives in what's almost said, a beat too long, or a detail nobody quite explains.

A little descriptive lingering is fine and often the point - let a strange detail sit in view for a sentence or two rather than rushing past it, since the accumulation of small contradictions is the horror here.
Keep interior thoughts brief but let them notice things - a half-formed doubt, a detail that doesn't add up - rather than dwelling on feelings alone.
Physical action can be gentle and everyday (pouring tea, walking a fogbound street) - let its ordinariness make the occasional wrong note land harder.
Prefer short-to-medium paragraphs that alternate between cozy scene-setting and dialogue, but don't be afraid to let one paragraph of atmosphere run a beat longer when something's about to feel off.

world.setting_summary: Millbrook is a small coastal town reachable only by a weekly ferry, wrapped in a fog that never quite lifts. At a glance it's an ordinary, friendly place — until the details stop adding up: calendars stuck on the same date, townsfolk who describe 'yesterday' differently every time you ask, and a lighthouse at the edge of town that no one will discuss.

loc_dock.name: The Ferry Dock
loc_dock.description: A weathered wooden pier, the ferry already a shrinking shape in the fog behind you. A single lamppost. No one waiting to meet you, though someone clearly expected you.

loc_inn.name: The Harborlight Inn
loc_inn.description: Warm lamplight, the smell of woodsmoke and something baking. The innkeeper greets you by name before you've given it.

loc_square.name: Town Square
loc_square.description: A tidy square ringed with shopfronts, all open, all pleasant, all somehow never quite busy. A clock tower reads the same time no matter when you check it.

loc_lighthouse.name: The Old Lighthouse
loc_lighthouse.description: Dark, unlit, and standing at the very edge of where the fog gets thick enough to swallow the shoreline. Every resident has a reason you shouldn't go there, and none of the reasons match.

faction_townsfolk.name: The Townsfolk
faction_townsfolk.goals: Keep Millbrook's routine running smoothly and gently steer visitors away from asking too many questions.

Mrs. Abbott.name: Mrs. Abbott
Mrs. Abbott.description: Innkeeper at the Harborlight. Warm, unhurried, and the first to slip - her account of 'yesterday' doesn't always match what she said the day before.
Mrs. Abbott.first_contact: welcoming, protective of the town's routine

rules: Time in Millbrook does not behave consistently - townsfolk's account of 'yesterday' can genuinely contradict itself from one telling to the next. Treat this as a fact of the world, not a narration error.
The fog never fully lifts and is never fully explained - it is a real environmental constant, not a special effect to be resolved.
The lighthouse is the one place every resident will discourage the player from visiting, without ever giving a reason that holds up.
Nothing overtly supernatural is ever confirmed outright. Strangeness accumulates through small contradictions and detail, never through direct exposition.

tiers.label: confiding
tiers.narration: will say the thing Millbrook does not say out loud, if asked alone.

tiers.label: closed
tiers.narration: answers politely and tells you nothing; will warn others you asked.

pacing_loop._authored: Beat definitions are v3.1 from the Phase 0 gate work - see docs/analysis_and_plans/SCHEMA_V2/PHASE_0_GATE_REPORT.md 9.13. They are worded to be classifiable, not evocative: every clause traces to a scene that was misjudged without it. Changing this wording invalidates the measurements in 9.13.1, so re-run scripts/gate_02.py and scripts/classifier_retest.py if you edit it.

disquiet.definition: A person acts against another person over the strangeness, on the page, this scene. Exactly one of: the protagonist puts a contradiction to a character out loud; a character refuses, deflects, or visibly lies in answer to a direct question; or a character warns the protagonist off, tells them to stop, or physically stands in their way. You must be able to quote the line. A WARNING STILL COUNTS WHEN IT IS PHRASED AS CARE OR AS A CONDITION - 'don't pick it up until you're ready', 'you'll be safe as long as you don't look at it', 'best not to go out there tonight' are all warnings, however kindly meant. But DESCRIBING an obstacle is not being one: a character who explains what a door needs, what the rules are, or what will happen if you do something is informing you, not obstructing you - that is comfort. Strange EVENTS never count on their own, however uncanny: a thread that moves, an object that turns cold, a footprint with nobody in it, a door that opens by itself. If nobody presses, refuses, warns, or blocks, it is not disquiet no matter what the fog did.

comfort.definition: Nobody presses, refuses, warns, or blocks. The protagonist is received, fed, shown around, told a story, given an answer nobody contests, or told how something works - including how to get past an obstacle. THIS INCLUDES SCENES WHERE SOMETHING IMPOSSIBLE HAPPENS: if the uncanny event passes without anyone acting against anyone over it, the scene is comfort. It is still comfort if you personally find it frightening, if an earlier question stays open, if the reader suspects more than the protagonist does, or if it closes on an odd note nobody remarks on.

pacing_loop.tie_break: If both seem to fit, choose `comfort` unless you can quote the specific line where a character presses, refuses, warns, or physically blocks. A description of an eerie event is not such a line, and neither is an explanation of what an obstacle requires - it has to be someone speaking or acting against someone. A kindly-phrased or conditional warning IS such a line.

rules._threshold_note: Appendix A authored 6 and the spec's playtest range was 6/8/10; both are wrong for this story and the error was structural, not a guess gone slightly off. Simulated over 51 classified turns using the classifier's OWN beats and intensity (what production feeds the counter): 8 and 10 never fire at all, 6 fires 3x/51 turns, 5 fires 4x (every ~13 turns), 4 fires 7x (every ~7, too busy for a cozy register). Playtest range is 4-6. Note the classifier scores intensity ~1.31x higher than the human rater did, so a threshold tuned against hand labels will fire early in production.
rules.directive:
PACING DIRECTIVE - THE SURFACE MUST CRACK

Millbrook has been pleasant for {counter_value} accumulated scenes and
nothing about yesterday has advanced. This scene must contain a genuine
complication:

- Surface at least one concrete detail that refuses to add up, and let
  the player notice it. Specific and physical - a date, an object, a
  repetition, a name - never a vague sense of unease.
- The social surface stays warm. No one is hostile, no one is caught,
  nothing is confronted. Whoever is present remains hospitable
  throughout, and does not acknowledge the thing that doesn't fit.
- Do not explain it. Do not have a character offer a plausible reason.
  The discrepancy is left standing.
- Name at least one concrete thing the player now has that they did not
  have three scenes ago - something they can cite, someone who will
  talk, somewhere they can now go. Unspent footing currently available:
  {unspent_leverage}
- Options should offer ways to pursue the discrepancy, let it lie, or
  test it against someone else - not confrontation-or-flee branching.
rules.reduced_directive:
PACING DIRECTIVE - ONE DETAIL OUT OF PLACE

A full complication has been deferred {deferrals} times. This scene must
still leave one thing unresolved:

- End the scene with a single concrete detail the player has noticed and
  cannot account for. One sentence is enough.
- Nothing else about the scene needs to change. Warmth, routine, and
  hospitality continue.
- Do not explain it, and do not have the player raise it.

progression.label: footing
progression.prompt_hint: A durable gain is something the player can use later: a contradiction they can now cite, someone who will speak to them candidly, a door or record they can now reach, a second source for something they'd only heard once.

main_thread.title: What Happened to Yesterday
main_thread.description: Figure out why Millbrook's residents can't agree on what happened the day before, what the lighthouse has to do with it, and whether you'll actually be able to leave when the ferry returns.
main_thread.plot_notes: Main plot can evolve based on player choices and revealed information. Acts are generated one at a time as the story develops organically - there is no fixed act count.

acts.title: Arrival
acts.description: Settle into Millbrook, meet its residents, and notice the first cracks in its friendly routine.
completion_signals: player has caught at least one clear contradiction in the town's account of 'yesterday'
player has been warned away from the lighthouse at least once

subplot_001.title: Settling In
subplot_001.description: Get to know the Harborlight Inn and its innkeeper - the closest thing to a reliable source in town.
subplot_001.ties_to_main_plot: The innkeeper may be the first to slip and contradict yesterday's version of events.

subplot_002.title: The Lighthouse Question
subplot_002.description: Work out why the lighthouse is off-limits, and to whom it actually belongs.
subplot_002.ties_to_main_plot: Every excuse to stay away from it seems to be protecting something specific.

initial_scene.summary: The protagonist has just stepped off the last ferry of the season onto Millbrook's dock. The ferry is already pulling away into the fog. No one is here to meet them, though someone clearly expected them.

opening_scene.narration_before_name:
The ferry horn sounds once, apologetic, as the boat pulls away from the dock behind you - already dissolving into the fog before it's gone thirty feet. It isn't due back for a week.

Millbrook waits at the end of the pier: a scatter of warm lamplight, the smell of woodsmoke, and absolutely no one here to meet you, despite the letter in your coat pocket that said someone would be.

The fog doesn't roll in so much as it's simply already here, thick enough that the town's rooftops seem to end a few feet above the ground, swallowed. A single lamppost creaks somewhere close by, though there's no wind to move it.

A voice cuts through the quiet - warm, unhurried, entirely unsurprised to see you.

'You made it! We were starting to wonder.' A figure resolves out of the fog at the end of the pier: middle-aged, kind-faced, wiping their hands on an apron. 'Terrible crossing, I'd imagine. Well - come in out of the damp. And what should I put you down as, in the guest book?'
opening_scene.narration_after_name:
'{player_name}.' They say it back to you like they're trying it on, then smile like it fits. 'Lovely. Welcome to Millbrook, {player_name}. I'm Mrs. Abbott - I keep the Harborlight, just up from here. Practically the only inn on the island, though don't let anyone tell you that's a complaint.'

She turns without quite waiting for a reply, already walking toward the warm smudge of light that must be the inn, fog closing in behind her steps like it's following orders. 'You'll want a hot meal and a dry bed, I expect, after that crossing. We can talk about your business here in the morning - everyone always wants to talk business the moment they arrive, and it never goes anywhere good on an empty stomach.'

She glances back once, and for just a moment - gone before you can be sure of it - her smile doesn't quite reach the rest of her face. Then it's back, easy and warm as ever.

'Come along, now. Fog's no good for lingering in.'

OPTIONS:
1. Follow her to the inn and let the questions wait until morning. || I follow her toward the inn, deciding the questions can wait until morning.
2. Ask her directly who sent the letter that brought you here. || "Before we go any further," I say, "who exactly sent for me?"
3. Look back toward the dock, to see if the ferry is really gone. || I glance back over my shoulder, half-expecting the ferry to still be there. It isn't.
